clinicalScope: Adult obesity (excess white adipose tissue) in East African and other low‑resource hospital settings
subject: Medicine
summary: Obesity is a disease of excess body fat caused by chronic energy imbalance. It is increasingly common in East Africa and brings metabolic, cardiovascular and surgical risks. This page guides clinicians through diagnosis, work‑up and management where resources are limited.

sections.p: Obesity is defined by a body mass index (BMI) ≥30 kg/m² or waist‑hip ratio >0.90 in men and >0.85 in women. Prevalence in urban East Africa is rising, now approaching 15‑20 % in adults, driven by nutrition transition and sedentary lifestyles.
b: BMI = weight (kg) ÷ height² (m²); easy to calculate at bedside.
Waist‑hip ratio adds central‑obesity information when scales are unavailable.
Obesity prevalence is higher in women and in middle‑aged groups (35‑55 y).
Rapid urbanisation correlates with increased fast‑food consumption.

sections.h: Causes and risk factors, most likely first
sections.p: In low‑resource settings, obesity often co‑exists with infections and socioeconomic changes.
b: High‑calorie, low‑nutrient diets (refined carbs, fried foods).
Physical inactivity (urban transport, desk jobs).
HIV‑associated lipodystrophy and antiretroviral therapy.
Tuberculosis or chronic infection causing altered appetite and later rebound weight gain.
Herbal remedies containing corticosteroids.
Genetic predisposition (family history, monogenic syndromes).
Socio‑economic factors: food insecurity leading to over‑consumption of cheap, energy‑dense foods.

sections.p: Excess caloric intake leads to hypertrophy and hyperplasia of white adipocytes, releasing adipokines that drive insulin resistance, inflammation and dyslipidaemia.
b: Positive energy balance → triglyceride storage in adipose tissue.
Adipocyte expansion releases leptin (satiety) and resistin (insulin resistance).
Chronic low‑grade inflammation via TNF‑α, IL‑6 promotes atherogenesis.
Visceral fat drains into portal circulation, worsening hepatic insulin resistance.
In HIV/TB, cytokine‑mediated catabolism followed by compensatory hyperphagia accelerates fat gain.

sections.p: Patients may be asymptomatic or present with metabolic, respiratory or musculoskeletal complaints.
b: Central (abdominal) obesity, waist circumference >102 cm (men) or >88 cm (women).
Acanthosis nigricans on neck or axillae indicating insulin resistance.
Barrel chest, reduced diaphragmatic excursion, exertional dyspnoea.
Joint pain, especially knees and lower back.
Fatigue, polyuria, nocturnal snoring suggestive of obstructive sleep apnoea.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: A focused history and physical exam uncover contributing factors and complications.
b: Ask about diet patterns, physical activity, recent infections (TB, HIV), medication (steroids, ART).
Screen for weight‑change trends, family history of diabetes or cardiovascular disease.
Measure weight, height, waist, hip; calculate BMI and waist‑hip ratio.
Inspect for acanthosis nigricans, striae, peripheral oedema.
Auscultate lungs for reduced breath sounds; assess gait and joint range.

sections.p: Conditions that mimic or coexist with obesity must be considered.
b: Cushing’s syndrome – central obesity with moon face, purple striae, hypertension.
Hypothyroidism – weight gain with cold intolerance, bradycardia.
Polycystic ovary syndrome – obesity, hirsutism, menstrual irregularities.
Lipodystrophy – loss of peripheral fat with central accumulation (often HIV‑related).
Edema from heart failure or nephrotic syndrome – pitting swelling without true fat gain.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Select tests that clarify metabolic risk and identify complications; adapt when resources are limited.

t.b: Detects diabetes or pre‑diabetes; ≥126 mg/dL = diabetes, 100‑125 mg/dL = pre‑diabetes.
Glycaemic control over 3 months; ≥6.5 % = diabetes. Use if laboratory HbA1c unavailable → rely on fasting glucose.
Assesses dyslipidaemia; LDL ≥130 mg/dL or triglycerides ≥150 mg/dL indicate high cardiovascular risk.
Hypertension defined as ≥140/90 mmHg; contributes to risk stratification.
Detects early diabetic or obesity‑related nephropathy; ≥1+ protein warrants further work‑up.
Evaluates cardiomegaly or pulmonary congestion secondary to obesity‑related heart failure.

sections.p: BMI categories guide risk assessment; waist circumference refines cardiovascular risk.
b: Class I: BMI 30‑34.9 kg/m² – moderate risk.
Class II: BMI 35‑39.9 kg/m² – high risk.
Class III: BMI ≥40 kg/m² – very high risk.
Add waist >102 cm (men) or >88 cm (women) → up‑stage by one class.

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, infections and medication side‑effects often intersect with obesity.
b: HIV antiretroviral therapy (protease inhibitors) → lipodystrophy, insulin resistance.
TB treatment (rifampicin) can alter hepatic metabolism of statins.
Herbal corticosteroids cause secondary obesity and hypertension.
Pregnancy‑related weight gain may mask baseline obesity.
Limited access to laboratory tests may delay detection of dysglycaemia.

sections.p: A tiered approach prioritises lifestyle, then pharmacotherapy, and finally referral for bariatric surgery when feasible.
b: 1️⃣ Counselling: calorie‑controlled diet (reduce refined carbs, increase vegetables/legumes), portion control using local foods.
2️⃣ Physical activity: ≥150 min/week moderate walking, community exercise groups.
3️⃣ Behavioural support: goal‑setting, self‑monitoring, peer groups.
4️⃣ Pharmacology (if BMI ≥30 kg/m² with comorbidity): metformin for insulin resistance; statin for dyslipidaemia; avoid thiazolidinediones (hepatotoxicity, limited monitoring).
5️⃣ Monitor: weight, waist, BP, fasting glucose every 3‑6 months.
6️⃣ Refer for bariatric surgery only in tertiary centres when BMI ≥40 kg/m² with uncontrolled comorbidities.

sections.p: Recognise acute or progressive problems that need urgent attention.
b: Sudden dyspnoea or chest pain → possible heart failure or pulmonary embolism.
Rapid weight loss, night sweats → consider TB or malignancy.
New‑onset hypertension or uncontrolled glucose → escalate pharmacotherapy.
Severe joint pain limiting mobility → evaluate for osteoarthritis or gout.

sections.p: Tailor management for populations with unique considerations.
b: Pregnant women – focus on gestational weight gain limits, screen for gestational diabetes.
HIV‑positive patients – monitor ART‑related metabolic effects, use metformin cautiously.
Elderly (>60 y) – avoid high‑impact exercise, watch for frailty and polypharmacy.
Children/adolescents – use BMI‑for‑age percentiles; prioritize family‑based lifestyle changes.

sections.p: Long‑term risk correlates with sustained BMI reduction; prevention starts early.
b: Weight loss ≥5 % improves insulin sensitivity and blood pressure.
Annual review of weight, waist, BP, glucose; more frequent if comorbid.
Community education on nutrition, active transport, and limiting sugary drinks.
School‑based programmes to instil healthy habits before adulthood.

sections.p: Interpretation pitfalls common in low‑resource contexts.
b: Normal fasting glucose may miss post‑prandial hyperglycaemia; consider HbA1c if available.
BMI underestimates adiposity in muscular individuals; use waist circumference as adjunct.
Low‑density lipoprotein (LDL) calculated by Friedewald formula can be inaccurate when triglycerides >400 mg/dL.
Edema from heart failure can be mistaken for obesity‑related weight gain.

whenToSeekHelp: Chest pain or severe shortness of breath
Sudden unexplained weight loss or night sweats
Acute swelling of one leg (possible deep vein thrombosis)
New onset confusion or altered mental status

faq.q: Is BMI the only way to diagnose obesity?
faq.a: No; waist‑hip ratio and clinical assessment of fat distribution are essential, especially when scales are unavailable.

faq.q: Can obesity be treated without medication?
faq.a: Yes; diet, physical activity and behavioural support are first‑line and can achieve meaningful weight loss in most patients.

faq.q: Why avoid thiazolidinediones in these settings?
faq.a: They can cause hepatotoxicity and fluid retention, which are hard to monitor without regular liver tests.

exam: What bedside measurements allow you to stage obesity and why are they important? — BMI and waist‑hip ratio; they predict cardiovascular and metabolic risk.

A 45‑year‑old woman with BMI 38 kg/m² presents with hypertension and acanthosis nigricans. Which investigation should you order first and what result would change management? — Fasting plasma glucose; ≥126 mg/dL would prompt adding metformin and tighter BP control.
How does HIV‑associated lipodystrophy differ from classic obesity on examination? — Loss of peripheral subcutaneous fat with central accumulation; may have a ‘buffalo hump’ and thinner limbs.

Explain the pathophysiological link between visceral fat and insulin resistance. — Visceral fat releases free fatty acids into portal circulation, impairing hepatic insulin signalling and increasing gluconeogenesis.
In a setting without lipid panels, how would you assess cardiovascular risk in an obese patient? — Use BMI class, waist circumference, blood pressure, and fasting glucose as surrogate markers.
Why is metformin preferred over thiazolidinediones for pre‑diabetes in low‑resource hospitals? — Metformin is inexpensive, has a good safety profile, and does not require liver function monitoring.

A patient with BMI 42 kg/m² develops sudden unilateral leg swelling. What is your next step and why? — Suspect deep vein thrombosis; order compression ultrasound if available, otherwise start empiric anticoagulation if high suspicion.
List three lifestyle interventions that are feasible in an East African urban clinic. — Portion control using local staples, walking groups, community cooking demonstrations with reduced oil.
How would you differentiate Cushing’s syndrome from simple obesity on exam? — Look for moon face, facial plethora, purple striae, proximal muscle weakness, and hypertension.
What red‑flag symptom in an obese patient warrants urgent evaluation for obstructive sleep apnoea? — Loud, witnessed apnoeic episodes or excessive daytime sleepiness with nocturnal choking.
Describe how TB infection can contribute to later obesity. — Chronic inflammation suppresses appetite; after treatment, rebound hyperphagia and reduced activity can lead to weight gain.

When is bariatric surgery indicated in low‑resource settings and what are the prerequisites? — BMI ≥40 kg/m² with uncontrolled comorbidities; requires multidisciplinary assessment, nutritional counselling, and postoperative follow‑up capacity.
